article_title: LOOKING AHEAD: THE WORK OF THE 1940 COUNCIL
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE SPRING, 1941
LOOKING AHEAD
THE WORK OF THE 1940 COUNCIL
WHEN internal development finally had its chance at the end of the last war, the vigour with which it was pursued was unaccompanied by the long-sighted planning necessary. Hence much of the confusion and unsightly building which has disfigured Britain in the last 20 years, despite many improvements in housing. It is quite obvious that reconstruction on a large scale will be necessary after this war, and it would be heading for chaos to wait until the millions of men and women are demobilised before finding out what their needs will be.

brief_context: Mentioned as an area needing decentralisation of industries.
article_title: LOOKING AHEAD: THE WORK OF THE 1940 COUNCIL
brief_extract: In planning for the future, the Grid has a vital part to play in improving the conditions of life and labour both in the industrial and domestic spheres. Electric power is available in all parts of the country, and because of this it is possible for the light industries to be made flexible and to be established in rural areas, thus achieving a measure of decentralisation which the big cities of the North and Midlands so urgently need. Indeed, in the heavy industries which must remain fixed electric power can provide a cleanliness and efficiency obtainable in no other way, and an atmosphere free from grime and smoke.

article_title: THE WORK OF WOMEN IN POLAND
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE SPRING, 1941

THE WORK OF WOMEN IN POLAND
By MADAME ALEKSANDRA PILSUDSKA

IN the days of my youth Polish women in their fight for emancipation had the same ends in view as the women of other nations: the equality of political rights with men, the right for intellectual work, and individual independence. After the restitution of Poland's independence, my husband, as the head of the State, when forming the new institutions, granted to the women of Poland rights equal to men, by a decree in 1919.

brief_context: Place of banishment for Polish women revolutionaries.
article_title: THE WORK OF WOMEN IN POLAND
brief_extract: We organised secret depots of illegal literature and of arms, we transported and delivered or hid arms, we taught Polish children the history of their country, a subject forbidden to them by the usurping Governments; we carried on social and revolutionary propaganda among the public at large. The reward for our work was prison, katorga, or banishment to Siberia — often death. The first world war found Polish women well prepared for the defence of the country.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the Polish war with Russia in 1920.
article_title: THE WORK OF WOMEN IN POLAND
brief_extract:
Women nursed the wounded as sisters of the Red Cross; as canteen workers and instructors in soldiers' clubs, they encouraged and strengthened the endurance of the men-folk in the stress of battle. During the Polish war with Russia in 1920, a war victorious for Poland, we saw Polish women standing as sentinels with a rifle in hand defending military stores and also fighting in the line as combatants. When caught by a merciless enemy they had to dig their own graves with their own hands; when led to execution they perished with the cry " Long live free Poland."
In free Poland, universities and academic schools were wide open to women, and no longer had they to go abroad in search of knowledge.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE. AUTUMN, 1941

THE WOMEN OF RUSSIA

“MY aunt is a bomber pilot”—this, the heading of a recent newspaper article, sounds strange to English ears, yet it is not surprising to the women of Russia who take their place side by side with men in every sphere of life. Under the Stalin Constitution they start level, as it guarantees them equal pay with men for equal work, and gives them equal opportunities and rights in every department of national and social life.

brief_context: City with large machinery plants and City Court.
brief_extract: There are over 170,000 women engineers in all branches of engineering, 650,000 women teachers, 73,000 women doctors, 9,000 women agronomists, and 33,000 women scientific workers. One woman was for three years chief of the research laboratory of one of the largest machinery plants in Moscow. In the Soviet Parliament there are 227 women deputies, in addition to thousands more in the local Soviets.
